ops.title: The mixed-era gate cannot certify itself from inside its own test package — phase 0 stops at the accident class
ops.body:
Four adversarial rounds against daemonkit's mixed-era release gate, 2026-07-29/30. Recording the
structural conclusion so a future session does not start round five.

## The gate kept failing the same way, four times

Its job: prove a release actually exercised the mixed-era matrix. DESIGN 8.4 makes it
non-waivable, because it is the one check that would have caught the swarm era's 18,999 handshake
failures — a wedge that hid behind green CI for five days because the test did not exist.

Every round moved the run's self-description somewhere new, and every new place was still inside
the thing being gated:

- R1: enforcement lived in a test's cleanup; `-count=0` on a tag exited PASS having run nothing.
- R2: an argument blocklist; `--run` and `GOFLAGS=-run=` walked past it, five cases silently
  skipped while the manifest reported full coverage.
- R3: an in-process ledger; a case whose body was replaced by its own bookkeeping passed, and
  deleting a case from the table deleted its requirement.
- R4: renamed the ledger writers to `observedPresent`/`observedAbsent` and called them observers.
  A case still writes its own evidence — they are package-level funcs and the cases are in the
  same package. All twelve cases emptied → exit 0, every cell PROVEN, no daemon started, no byte
  on a wire.

R4's front doors were forgeable too, without touching the observer files: `newRelay` takes a
caller-chosen upstream (point it at your own echo server, replay the checked-in fixture),
`peer` is a plain struct so `runPeer` execs whatever binary you name (`/bin/echo` passes), and
`assertPreambleCrossed` takes a caller-built exchange list and only sets `preambled = true`,
after which any clean exit is attributed to the preamble.

## The structural reason, stated once

**A Go test package cannot certify itself against its own package.** Anything in
`package mixedera` can call anything else in it, so any observer boundary drawn inside it is a
naming convention. Four rounds of moving the boundary around inside the package could not fix
that and a fifth would not either.

The real fix is process separation: the run emits raw artifacts, and a SEPARATE verifier binary —
not linkable from the test — reads them and renders the verdict. A case cannot call a function
that is not in its address space.

## Why that fix is deferred to phase 2, not done now

The cut-era peer is a phase-0 STUB. `GITHUB_REF_TYPE=tag ./scripts/mixed-era.sh` exits 1 even on
a fully green run, correctly, because the cut era's real transport is not under test yet — so the
gate's actual teeth have never been green once. Hardening a gate against a determined author
while its subject does not exist is the wrong order, and the R4 patch additionally wired
`mixed-era` into `release.yml`'s `needs:`, which would have failed the next tag push for a reason
true and unfixable until phase 2.

## What phase 0 closes instead: the accident class

Every surviving attack required deliberately editing case bodies to feed observers fabricated
inputs. That is not the threat. The threat is accidental narrowing, and three reported holes were
squarely in it:

1. **Silent claim deletion.** Deleting `wedge/18999`'s claim lines and emptying its body is green
   AND leaves the coverage table unchanged, because other cases re-prove those mechanisms. The
   case reproducing the original incident becomes an empty function with no report anywhere.
2. **Case-only lines.** `skew/build` and `classify/cut` appear in the frozen file with no claims,
   so their bodies empty with zero signal and no file edit.
3. **The era is a label.** `buildPeer(t, era, directive)` takes the era name and the go.mod
   directive as independent strings; pointing precut at the working tree makes both eras the same
   tree while the summary still prints "Boundary release v0.20.10". This is what someone does to
   make a build error go away.

Plus a credibility problem: 4 of 13 full-matrix runs went red purely on the pre-cut trust-probe
flake (the fork/exec latency of note a40a3a1). A ~30% false-red rate teaches people to re-run
without reading, which is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

## The standing rule

The gate's boundary is now written in `ci/mixedera/coverage_test.go` itself, where the next
contributor meets it: it catches accidental narrowing — a filtered run, a deleted case, an
orphaned requirement, an emptied body, a peer built against the wrong era — and it does not catch
a case that deliberately feeds the observers fabricated inputs. An honest boundary written where
it will be read beats a fifth round of whack-a-mole and a claim that does not hold.

Phase 2 restores the `release.yml` edge and moves the verdict out of process, when the cut peer
stops being a stub.
